headings.title: Introduction to Blood Pressure
headings.content: Blood pressure is the physical force exerted by circulating blood against the inner walls of the body's arteries. As the heart muscle pumps, it creates two distinct pressures measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). **Systolic pressure** represents the peak arterial pressure during heart contraction, while **diastolic pressure** reflects the lowest pressure remaining in the arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Understanding these two values helps nurses evaluate how efficiently the cardiovascular system delivers oxygen-rich blood to vital organs across the body.

headings.title: Physiology and Mechanisms of Blood Pressure Regulation
headings.content: Maintaining stable blood pressure requires a complex coordination between cardiac output, peripheral vascular resistance, and blood volume. Short-term regulation relies heavily on the **autonomic nervous system** and baroreceptors located in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch, which detect stretch and adjust heart rate instantly. Long-term regulation is primarily managed by the kidneys through the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)**, adjusting fluid balance and sodium retention to stabilize pressure over days.

headings.title: Classification and Normal Ranges of Blood Pressure
headings.content:
Blood pressure categories guide clinical diagnosis and treatment plans. Readings are interpreted using both systolic and diastolic values.

- **Normal**: Systolic under 120 and diastolic under 80 mmHg.
- **Elevated**: Systolic 120 to 129 and diastolic under 80 mmHg.
- **Hypertension Stage 1**: Systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89 mmHg.
- **Hypertension Stage 2**: Systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90 mmHg.
- **Hypertensive Crisis**: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120 mmHg.

headings.title: Techniques for Accurate Blood Pressure Assessment
headings.content: Accurate measurement is critical for preventing misdiagnosis and improper treatment. Using a cuff of incorrect size introduces significant error—a cuff that is too small yields falsely high readings, while one that is too large gives falsely low results. The patient should rest quietly for five minutes with feet flat on the floor and the arm supported at heart level before inflation. The stethoscope bell is placed gently over the brachial artery, avoiding excessive pressure that can artificially silence **Korotkoff sounds**.

headings.title: Hypertension: Causes, Risk Factors, and Pathophysiology
headings.content: Most cases are classified as **primary hypertension**, meaning there is no single identifiable medical cause, though genetics, aging, and lifestyle heavily contribute. **Secondary hypertension** results from an underlying condition such as renal artery stenosis, endocrine disorders, or medication side effects. Persistent high pressure causes vascular remodeling, stiffening arterial walls, and increasing the workload of the left ventricle over time.

headings.title: Hypotension: Causes and Clinical Implications
headings.content: Hypotension is generally defined as a systemic blood pressure reading below 90/60 mmHg, though many healthy adults normally run low without symptoms. When inadequate perfusion occurs, vital organs are starved of oxygen and nutrients. **Orthostatic hypotension** occurs when a sudden drop in pressure happens upon standing up, often linked to dehydration, prolonged bed rest, or autonomic dysfunction.

headings.title: Pharmacological and Non-Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Managing blood pressure often requires a combination of lifestyle changes and medications. Non-pharmacological approaches include adopting the DASH diet rich in fruits and vegetables, reducing sodium intake, engaging in regular aerobic exercise, and limiting alcohol consumption. When drugs are necessary, common classes include **diuretics**, **ACE inhibitors**, **beta-blockers**, and **calcium channel blockers**, tailored to individual patient needs and comorbidities.

headings.title: Complications of Untreated Blood Pressure Disorders
headings.content: Chronic, poorly controlled hypertension places excessive mechanical stress on the circulatory system, leading to widespread end-organ damage. Over time, weakened arterial walls can balloon into aneurysms or rupture, causing hemorrhagic strokes. The heart hypertrophies to push against high resistance, eventually leading to heart failure, while damaged renal microvasculature results in chronic kidney disease and eventual renal failure.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Education
headings.content: Nurses play a vital role in monitoring blood pressure trends, identifying adverse drug effects, and guiding patients toward sustainable lifestyle changes. Education focuses on teaching proper home blood pressure monitoring techniques, emphasizing adherence to prescribed medication regimens even when asymptomatic, and recognizing warning signs of cardiovascular distress such as severe headaches, chest pain, or sudden dizziness.
